title: Colombia's Fuzzy Plants Guard the Water
summary: High in the mountains of Colombia, Moisés Moreno grows tiny plants in a greenhouse. They are called frailejones, and they can grow to be 30 feet tall. They are related to the sunflower. They grow in the páramos, the high, wet lands of the mountains. The soft fuzz on their leaves keeps them warm and soaks up water from clouds. That water feeds rivers and gives much of Colombia its water. The plants are named for monks in hoods, and the Muisca people saw them as sacred guardians of the water. But today the plants are in danger. Of nearly 150 kinds, two-thirds are at risk, and 17 are endangered. Farmers, ranchers, and miners are moving higher up, and a warming climate lets new plants grow where they could not before. Moreno knows this well. As a young man, he cut frailejones down to make fields for potatoes and cows. Later, after he was hurt in a coal mine, he decided to protect the mountains instead. Now he leads volunteers who hike to 11,000 feet to plant tiny frailejones. Many die in the cold, and the ones that live grow only a few inches a year.
why_it_matters: The water you drink can depend on plants like these, far away in the mountains.
